addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

1	import Foundation
2	import OpenAPIRuntime
3	import OSLog
4	
5	/// Everything that turns a thrown error into something a person reads, in one
6	/// place: the sentence itself, whether there is anything to say at all, and the
7	/// log line that survives either way.
8	public extension RobotSession {
9	    /// `ReachyKitError` carries actionable text; raw interpolation would print
10	    /// the bare case name instead.
11	    ///
12	    /// The generated client wraps transport failures in a `ClientError` whose
13	    /// description carries the whole operation context — around twenty lines of
14	    /// `NSError` internals that bury the one sentence worth reading. Unwrap to the
15	    /// root cause first, so a refused connection reads as "Could not connect to
16	    /// the server."
17	    /// Public because a session is not the only thing that has to put a daemon
18	    /// failure in front of someone: an App Intent gets one line in Shortcuts and
19	    /// no screen to elaborate on.
20	    /// `nonisolated` because it reads only its argument: an intent runs off the
21	    /// main actor and still has to render the same sentence.
22	    nonisolated static func describe(_ error: Error) -> String {
23	        let root = rootCause(of: error)
24	        return (root as? LocalizedError)?.errorDescription ?? root.localizedDescription
25	    }
26	
27	    /// The sentence to show for a failed daemon call, or `nil` when there is
28	    /// nothing worth showing. Logs either way, and is the **only** place that
29	    /// does — a second logging point in the funnels would double every line.
30	    ///
31	    /// Every screen that displays a daemon failure goes through this rather than
32	    /// through `describe` directly. That is not a style preference: a cancelled
33	    /// request reads as the word "cancelled" (see `isCancellation`), so a model
34	    /// left to describe its own errors puts it on its own tab instead. Moving the
35	    /// filter into the session alone would have moved the bug, not fixed it.
36	    ///
37	    /// `nil` means *leave what is on screen alone*. An abandoned call learned
38	    /// nothing, so it may neither report a failure nor clear one still being read.
39	    nonisolated static func message(for error: Error) -> String? {
40	        guard !isCancellation(error) else {
41	            // `.public`: an error description carries no user data, and a line
42	            // reading `<private>` would defeat the point of keeping it.
43	            log.debug("dropped cancelled call: \(String(describing: error), privacy: .public)")
44	            return nil
45	        }
46	        let message = describe(error)
47	        log.error("daemon call failed: \(message, privacy: .public)")
48	        return message
49	    }
50	
51	    /// A cancelled call is not a robot failure — it is this app letting go. The
52	    /// screen that asked went away, or the session was torn down under an
53	    /// in-flight request; either way nobody is waiting for the answer and the
54	    /// robot did nothing wrong.
55	    ///
56	    /// It has to be recognised by code, never by text: `URLSession` reports an
57	    /// abandoned task as `NSURLErrorCancelled` whose entire localized description
58	    /// is the single word **"cancelled"**, and `describe` faithfully passed that
59	    /// word on. Opening the Apps tab and leaving again before the catalogue
60	    /// arrived was all it took to print it in red monospace on the robot screen.
61	    nonisolated static func isCancellation(_ error: Error) -> Bool {
62	        switch rootCause(of: error) {
63	        case is CancellationError: true
64	        case let urlError as URLError: urlError.code == .cancelled
65	        default: false
66	        }
67	    }
68	}
69	
70	extension RobotSession {
71	    private nonisolated static let log = Logger(
72	        subsystem: "com.alexey1312.ReachyMini",
73	        category: "RobotSession"
74	    )
75	
76	    private nonisolated static func rootCause(of error: Error) -> Error {
77	        if let clientError = error as? ClientError {
78	            return rootCause(of: clientError.underlyingError)
79	        }
80	        return error
81	    }
82	
83	    /// Records a connection or power failure in `robotError` — the session's own
84	    /// slot, and the only kind of failure entitled to it. A feature's funnel
85	    /// throws and says nothing here; its screen owns the message.
86	    func report(_ error: Error) {
87	        guard let message = Self.message(for: error) else { return }
88	        robotError = message
89	    }
90	}
91

1	import Foundation
2	import Observation
3	import ReachyKit
4	
5	/// The robot's two destructive maintenance actions: clearing the Hugging Face
6	/// cache and uninstalling every app.
7	///
8	/// A model rather than `@State` on the card, because the interesting part is not
9	/// the two calls but the rule in front of one of them — and that rule is worth
10	/// asserting without a view.
11	@MainActor
12	@Observable
13	final class MaintenanceModel {
14	    enum Action: Equatable, Identifiable, CaseIterable {
15	        case clearHuggingFaceCache
16	        case resetApps
17	
18	        var id: Self {
19	            self
20	        }
21	    }
22	
23	    /// What the confirmation dialog is asking about. Not `private(set)` — the
24	    /// dialog's binding writes it back on dismissal.
25	    var confirming: Action?
26	    private(set) var running: Action?
27	    /// The last action that finished cleanly, so the card can say so in place.
28	    private(set) var finished: Action?
29	    private(set) var lastError: String?
30	
31	    var isBusy: Bool {
32	        running != nil
33	    }
34	
35	    /// Uninstalling every app is `shutil.rmtree("/venvs/apps_venv/")`, and the
36	    /// daemon neither stops a running app first nor puts anything back — the
37	    /// interpreter a live app is executing in simply goes away underneath it.
38	    /// The robot offers no protection there, so this is the client's, and the
39	    /// card says which app to stop rather than only greying the button out.
40	    ///
41	    /// An unfamiliar process state counts as running, the same way
42	    /// `RobotAppStatus.State.isBusy` treats it: refusing to delete an
43	    /// environment that might be in use is the safe way to be wrong.
44	    func blockingApp(_ session: RobotSession) -> RobotApp? {
45	        guard let status = session.runningApp, status.isBusy else { return nil }
46	        return status.app
47	    }
48	
49	    func perform(_ action: Action, session: RobotSession) async {
50	        running = action
51	        finished = nil
52	        lastError = nil
53	        defer { running = nil }
54	        do {
55	            switch action {
56	            case .clearHuggingFaceCache: try await session.clearHuggingFaceCache()
57	            case .resetApps: try await session.resetApps()
58	            }
59	            finished = action
60	            // What the session last saw about installed apps is fiction now: the
61	            // venv every one of them lived in has just been deleted. Failing to
62	            // re-read is not worth reporting — the dock polls this anyway, and
63	            // the delete itself succeeded.
64	            if action == .resetApps {
65	                try? await session.refreshCurrentApp()
66	            }
67	        } catch {
68	            lastError.recordDaemonFailure(error)
69	        }
70	    }
71	}
72	
73	#if DEBUG
74	    extension MaintenanceModel {
75	        /// In the model's own file rather than in `Previews/`: it writes
76	        /// `private(set)` members, which `@testable` does not reach.
77	        static func preview(
78	            confirming: Action? = nil,
79	            running: Action? = nil,
80	            finished: Action? = nil,
81	            error: String? = nil
82	        ) -> MaintenanceModel {
83	            let model = MaintenanceModel()
84	            model.confirming = confirming
85	            model.running = running
86	            model.finished = finished
87	            model.lastError = error
88	            return model
89	        }
90	    }
91	#endif

Based on my review of the changed files, I traced each security-relevant change:

1. **AppSettingsScreen.swift `report(_:)`** — Changed from `!RobotSession.isCancellation` + `describe` to `RobotSession.message(for:)`. Verified `message(for:)` in `RobotSession+Errors.swift`: it does the same cancellation filter and adds a `privacy: .public` log line. Since the WKWebView is loading a local-network app-settings URL (`extra["custom_app_url"]`, port-only per the docstring) with no embedded tokens, the added log is not a sensitive-to-observability finding.

2. **CacheMaintenanceClient.swift `resetApps()`** — Adds cache invalidation (`appCatalogueCache = nil; installedAppsCache = nil`) after the destructive call. This is a stale-data correctness fix (avoids offering Open/Remove on deleted apps), not a security regression. No injection/authz surface.

3. **PreviewFixtures.swift** — Adds `CacheMaintenanceClient` conformance to `PreviewRobotClient` inside `#if DEBUG`. Both methods throw `wirelessFeaturesUnavailable`; nothing exec-shaped, no filesystem sink, and the whole file is DEBUG-gated so it cannot ship.

4. **MaintenanceCard.swift / MaintenanceModel.swift** — Pure formatting/whitespace changes and an explicit `case .clearHuggingFaceCache, .none` instead of `default`. No behavioural change.

5. **PreviewScenes.swift / PreviewSettingsScenes.swift / AppSettingsPreviews.swift** — File split (moved existing scene builders to a new file). All preview-only code.

6. **Tests/** — Additions to `AppsRobotClient` (test double gains a `resetAppsCalls` counter and `CacheMaintenanceClient` conformance) and new tests. Test-only.

No entry-point / sink pairs, authorization gates, parsers, or trust boundaries are introduced or altered in a way that enables an attacker-influenceable path. The Phase 2c checklist (sensitive-to-observability, allowlist escapes, gate/action mismatches, control regressions, IaC omitted args, CI/CD trust, over-broad grants, stale identity, fail-open state drift, security-registry fanout, under-validated sink args, resource caps) has no matches against the + lines.
